question: What are the two primary physiological functions of the ovaries?

options.B: Production of oocytes and secretion of sex hormones

explanation: The ovaries serve the dual primary functions of producing oocytes and secreting female sex hormones like estrogen and progesterone. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h1)

question: Why is ovarian cancer frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage based on its anatomy?

options.A: The ovaries are heavily encapsulated by thick bone barriers.
options.C: Ovaries lack anatomical barriers in the pelvic cavity, allowing cells to shed easily into the peritoneum.
options.D: The germinal epithelium prevents any cellular growth.

explanation: Because the ovaries are suspended freely in the pelvic cavity without anatomical barriers, malignant cells can readily shed into the peritoneal cavity early on. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h1)

question: Which histological type accounts for the majority (85-90%) of all ovarian cancer cases?
explanation: Epithelial ovarian carcinomas are the most common histological type, representing about 85 to 90 percent of all diagnoses. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h2)

question: How do malignant ovarian cells commonly achieve transcoelomic spread?

options.A: By exfoliating into peritoneal fluid and seeding across the peritoneal surface
options.B: By traveling exclusively through the arterial blood supply
options.C: By migrating up the ureters into the kidneys
options.D: By direct invasion through the abdominal skin

explanation: Transcoelomic spread occurs when malignant cells exfoliate into the peritoneal fluid and seed across the peritoneal cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h2)

question: Which genetic mutations are strongly linked to an increased risk of hereditary ovarian cancer?
explanation: Inherited mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are the most well-known genetic risk factors for developing ovarian cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h3)

question: Which of the following factors is considered protective against the development of ovarian cancer?
explanation: Oral contraceptives suppress ovulation, which reduces the lifetime number of ovulatory cycles and provides a protective effect against ovarian cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h3)

question: Why is early-stage ovarian cancer notoriously difficult to diagnose based on its symptoms?

options.A: It causes immediate and severe paralysis.
options.B: It presents with vague, non-specific symptoms that mimic gastrointestinal or urinary conditions.
options.C: It is always accompanied by high fevers and jaundice.
options.D: It presents exclusively as a skin rash.

explanation: Early symptoms like bloating and pelvic pain are vague and often mistaken for common gastrointestinal or urinary issues. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h4)

question: Which symptom is characteristic of advanced ovarian cancer involving peritoneal dissemination?
explanation: Advanced disease often causes peritoneal fluid accumulation (ascites), leading to marked abdominal distension and discomfort. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h4)

question: Which serum tumor marker is most commonly monitored in suspected epithelial ovarian cancer?
explanation: CA-125 is the primary serum tumor marker used in the evaluation and monitoring of epithelial ovarian cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h5)

question: Why is CA-125 alone insufficient for definitively diagnosing ovarian cancer?

options.A: It is only present in male patients.
options.B: It can be elevated in benign conditions like endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease.
options.C: It is completely absent in 100% of advanced cancer cases.
options.D: It degrades rapidly before blood samples can be analyzed.

explanation: CA-125 levels can rise in various benign conditions, meaning it lacks absolute specificity for cancer diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h5)

question: In the FIGO staging system, what does Stage III ovarian cancer signify?

options.A: Cancer is strictly confined to one ovary.
options.B: Cancer involves the uterus and fallopian tubes only.
options.C: Cancer has spread beyond the pelvis to the abdominal peritoneum and/or retroperitoneal lymph nodes.
options.D: Distant metastasis to the brain or bone has occurred.

explanation: Stage III ovarian cancer indicates that the disease has spread outside the pelvis into the abdominal peritoneum and/or local lymph nodes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h6)

question: What does tumor grading evaluate in ovarian cancer?

options.A: The exact age of the patient at diagnosis
options.B: The cellular differentiation and aggressiveness of the tumor cells
options.C: The total volume of ascites fluid present
options.D: The patient's response to pain medication

explanation: Tumor grading assesses how differentiated and aggressive the cancer cells appear microscopically compared to normal tissue. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h6)

question: What is the primary objective of surgical debulking (cytoreduction) in ovarian cancer?

options.A: To remove all reproductive organs while preserving hormonal function indefinitely
options.B: To remove as much tumor mass as possible, leaving minimal or no visible residual disease
options.C: To replace the peritoneal cavity with synthetic mesh
options.D: To harvest stem cells for autologous bone marrow transplant

explanation: Optimal debulking aims to remove macroscopic tumor burden so that little to no visible residual disease remains, improving survival. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h7)

question: Which combination chemotherapy regimen is standard practice following surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer?
explanation: Platinum-based therapy using carboplatin combined with paclitaxel is the standard systemic chemotherapy regimen for epithelial ovarian cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h7)

question: What is a critical nursing responsibility during a patient's course of chemotherapy for ovarian cancer?

options.A: Monitoring for myelosuppression and signs of infection

explanation: Chemotherapy causes bone marrow suppression (myelosuppression), making close monitoring for infection and bleeding precautions a vital nursing duty. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h8)

question: Why is holistic psychological and emotional support essential in ovarian cancer nursing care?

options.A: It guarantees the tumor will spontaneously regress.
options.B: Treatments profoundly impact reproductive capacity, body image, and sexual health.
options.C: It replaces the need for surgical interventions.
options.D: Psychological support eliminates the side effects of chemotherapy.

explanation: Ovarian cancer treatments alter reproductive organs and body image, causing significant psychological distress that requires empathetic nursing support. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h8)

question: Which complication is commonly caused by tumor compression or extensive peritoneal adhesions in advanced ovarian cancer?
explanation: Tumor compression and peritoneal adhesions frequently lead to malignant bowel obstruction in advanced stages of the disease. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h9)

question: How does the stage of diagnosis primarily affect the prognosis of ovarian cancer?

options.A: Stage has no correlation with survival outcomes.
options.B: Localized Stage I disease has a significantly higher five-year survival rate compared to advanced stages.
options.C: Advanced stages always have a better prognosis than early stages.
options.D: Prognosis depends solely on the patient's geographic location.

explanation: Patients diagnosed at localized Stage I have a much higher five-year survival rate than those diagnosed at advanced, widespread stages. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T33#GNS216_U5_T33_h9)
